+Step-down transfers shared-write responsibility without restarting the old leader and changes
+it to a follower. After the transition, the node reads its stable tables through read-only views
+of the concluding checkpoint, so every change it must still serve has to be either in that
+checkpoint or in its ingest tables. The application therefore needs a clear boundary between
+writes that belong in the concluding checkpoint handed to the next leader and later writes that
+must be stored locally for follower operations. There are two ways to establish it.
+@subsection disagg-step-down-blocking Blocking step-down
+The simplest boundary is to stop writing. In blocking step-down, writes stop while the
+concluding checkpoint is taken and remain stopped through the reconfiguration. Until
+reconfiguration, the node still operates as a leader and writes to its live stable tables.
+Reconfiguration switches those tables to read-only checkpoint views, so updates newer than the
+checkpoint would no longer be available through the follower's stable tables. The concluding
+checkpoint's latency therefore becomes part of the period in which the application cannot write.
+@subsection disagg-step-down-async Asynchronous step-down
+Asynchronous step-down defines the boundary in advance so writes can continue while the
+concluding checkpoint is taken. The application sets a step-down timestamp N, and transactions
+that begin after it is set keep a copy of their writes in the ingest tables. The concluding
+checkpoint is taken at N, so the node can switch to checkpointed stable table views without
+losing newer writes. Writes must still stop for the step-down reconfiguration itself, so
+asynchronous step-down shortens the period of write unavailability but does not eliminate it.
+The rest of this section describes how writes are routed while N is set, why some transactions
+are rolled back, how reads and schema operations behave, and what the reconfiguration does.
+@subsection disagg-step-down-routing Write routing
+WiredTiger chooses the destination of a transaction's writes using the step-down state recorded
+at transaction begin. A transaction that began before N was set writes to the stable tables
+only. A transaction that began after N was set writes to the ingest tables, and in the default
+mode to the stable tables as well.
+Writes above N must be retained in the ingest tables because they are not included in the
+concluding checkpoint. After the step-down reconfiguration, stable-table reads use the read-only
+checkpoint view, so those newer writes must remain available in the ingest tables.
+The disaggregated=(stepdown_write_mirroring) setting of ::wiredtiger_open selects
+between the two modes for transactions that begin after N. For applications, the modes differ
+mainly in the write-conflict detection they guarantee: mirrored writes detect every conflict at
+the conflicting write, as outside a step-down, while ingest-only writes can miss a conflict with
+a straddling writer until that writer is rolled back.
+- Mirrored writes (default): each write to an existing layered table goes to the stable
+  table first and then to the ingest table, within the same transaction. Because every writer,
+  including those that began before N was set, writes to the stable table, WiredTiger's normal
+  single-btree conflict detection handles conflicts between them. The stable table versions
+  above N are excluded from the concluding checkpoint by its timestamp.
+- Ingest-only writes (legacy): writes go to the ingest tables only. Writers on the two
+  sides of the boundary no longer share an update chain, so each ingest-only write performs an
+  explicit check against the stable table for conflicting updates. This check does not always
+  detect conflicts immediately with writers that began before N was set and straddle setting
+  the step-down timestamp. Those writers are rolled back rather than committed, so the missed
+  conflicts cannot persist.
+In both modes, the ingest table holds the copy that survives the step-down reconfiguration.
+Mirroring trades additional stable table writes and reconciliation for immediate conflict
+detection through a single btree; ingest-only writes avoid the extra copy but rely on the
+cross-table check.
+@subsection disagg-step-down-transactions Why straddling writers are rolled back
+WiredTiger chooses the destination of transaction writes using the step-down state recorded at
+transaction begin for two reasons:
+1. A transaction can set its commit timestamp after it has already written, and the write cannot
+   be moved to the alternative table afterwards. A write with a commit timestamp at or below N
+   belongs in the stable table, so the destination needs to be chosen before the relevant commit
+   timestamp exists.
+2. Straddler rollback keeps each transaction's write destinations consistent with its begin-time
+   state, so the state recorded at begin provides the correct destination for every write of
+   that transaction.
+A layered-table write checks whether the transaction began before N was set and returns
+WT_ROLLBACK when it observes the change, failing the transaction early. The commit path also
+checks for straddling writers and is synchronized with setting the step-down timestamp. Under
+the application contract, this ensures such writers cannot commit above N. A retried transaction
+begins with N set and writes to the ingest tables.
+@subsection disagg-step-down-reads Reads during step-down
+Reads follow the same decision made at transaction begin. This is possible because layered-table
+operations always run in explicit snapshot-isolation transactions, and WT_SESSION::reset_snapshot
+is not allowed while the step-down timestamp is set. A transaction that began after N was set
+reads the ingest table layered over the still-live stable table. One that began earlier reads
+the stable table alone, which already holds everything its snapshot can see. The decision stays
+correct only while the transaction keeps reading the state it saw at begin.
+The step-down reconfiguration replaces each live stable table with a view of the concluding
+checkpoint. The checkpoint keeps older versions in the shared history store, which supports
+reads at a timestamp, so a transaction with a read timestamp selects the same versions from the
+checkpoint view. A transaction without a read timestamp that straddles reconfiguration may be
+rolled back because its snapshot cannot be assumed to select consistent content from the
+replacement.
+@subsection disagg-step-down-schema Schema changes during step-down
+A layered table created after N is set has the follower table shape: only its local ingest
+table is created. Writes to such a table always go to the ingest table and are never mirrored,
+so a stable table would stay empty, and the concluding checkpoint must not include the table.
+Without schema epochs, the concluding checkpoint applies every other schema operation queued
+when it starts, including drops issued after N was set. With schema epochs, the step-down epoch
+divides schema operations the same way N divides data. See @ref disagg_role_management_schema
+for the schema-epoch contract.

+/*! @page disagg_role_management Managing disaggregated storage roles
+In disaggregated storage, the application decides which node owns shared writes and coordinates
+elections, replication, and the handoff between nodes. WiredTiger provides leader and follower
+roles so the application can choose which node persists data to shared storage without
+restarting the connections.
+This page describes roles from the application's perspective, including configuration,
+expected call sequences, and restrictions. See @ref arch-disagg-roles for their architecture
+and implementation.
+@section disagg_role_management_roles Leader and follower
+There are two roles: the leader and the follower.
+The leader accepts application writes and persists their changes in shared storage through
+checkpoints. A follower accepts replicated writes and stores their changes locally,
+without persisting them to shared storage. Both serve reads from shared data: a leader reads the
+current data, while a follower reads the most recent checkpoint it adopted, together with newer
+replicated changes it applied locally.
+| Responsibility | Leader | Follower |
+| Accepted writes | Application writes | Writes replicated from the leader |
+| Where changes are persisted | Shared storage through checkpoints | Not persisted to shared storage by this node |
+| Readable data | Current data | Shared checkpointed data and newer local changes |
+| Shared checkpoints | Produces them | Adopts checkpoints produced by the leader |
+Once an adopted checkpoint contains a change, the follower can remove its local copy when it is
+no longer needed by readers. Frequent leader checkpoints and follower checkpoint adoption
+therefore reduce the amount of data followers must retain locally. A local copy is not removed
+merely because a checkpoint was produced; the follower must first adopt it, and removal must be
+safe for existing readers.
+Keeping changes locally does not persist them to shared storage. Applications remain
+responsible for replication and for replaying changes needed after a restart.

+@section disagg_role_management_changes Changing a node's role
+The application changes a node's role using WT_CONNECTION::reconfigure with
+disaggregated=(role=...). There are two role changes: step-up changes a follower
+into a leader, and step-down changes a leader into a follower. Reconfiguration performs
+the local storage-engine transition, not the election or replication of changes to another node.
+The application must prevent competing shared writers and satisfy the transaction and checkpoint
+requirements of each role change.
+@section disagg_role_management_handoff Handing off shared writes
+Moving shared-write responsibility from one node to another combines a step-down on the old
+leader with a step-up on the new one. The last shared checkpoint the old leader takes before
+stepping down is the concluding checkpoint; it is the base from which the new leader
+continues. A complete handoff usually proceeds as follows:
+1. The old leader takes the concluding checkpoint and steps down, as described in
+   @ref disagg_role_management_step_down.
+2. The application passes the concluding checkpoint's metadata to the node that will become the
+   new leader, which adopts it through WT_CONNECTION::reconfigure with
+ disaggregated=(checkpoint_meta=...).
+3. The new leader steps up, as described in @ref disagg_role_management_step_up. The old leader
+   can write to shared storage until its step-down reconfiguration completes, so the new leader
+   must not step up before then.
+4. Data writes and schema operations not included in the concluding checkpoint are applied on
+   the new leader, either before step-up as replicated follower writes or after it as leader
+   writes. Retaining them locally on the old leader does not transfer them to another node.
+Step 4 applies whether or not schema epochs are used: schema epochs select which schema
+operations a checkpoint includes, but do not replace replication. The application must make the
+corresponding schema available before applying data writes that depend on it.
+The diagram shows one asynchronous handoff in which the next leader adopts the checkpoint
+while still a follower, before the old leader completes its step-down. The example omits schema
+epochs; their additional settings are described in @ref disagg_role_management_schema.

+@section disagg_role_management_step_up Step-up
+Step-up is initiated by calling WT_CONNECTION::reconfigure with
+disaggregated=(role=leader) on a follower. After the call completes, the node can
+accept leader writes and produce shared checkpoints for the disaggregated database.
+@subsection disagg_role_management_step_up_requirements Requirements
+Transactions and positioned cursors must not span step-up. The application must finish
+transactions and reset or close positioned cursors before the step-up reconfiguration.
+@subsection disagg_role_management_step_up_flow Usual flow
+The usual flow of step-up is:
+1. Finish transactions and reset or close positioned cursors.
+2. Ensure the follower has adopted the concluding checkpoint and has applied the replicated
+   operations needed for it to become the new leader.
+3. Call WT_CONNECTION::reconfigure with disaggregated=(role=leader).
+4. Start new leader operations after reconfiguration completes.
+@section disagg_role_management_step_down Step-down
+Step-down changes a leader into a follower by calling WT_CONNECTION::reconfigure with
+disaggregated=(role=follower). The node stops persisting shared writes and instead
+stores replicated changes locally while continuing to read shared checkpointed data.
+Every change the node accepted as leader must end up either in the concluding checkpoint or in a
+local copy that survives the reconfiguration. The application chooses between two ways of
+drawing that boundary: blocking step-down stops writes while the concluding checkpoint is
+taken, while asynchronous step-down declares the boundary in advance so writes can continue
